Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.4.1/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

## Establish Shared Understanding

The outcome of brainstorming is an understanding your human partner can
recognize and correct, grounded in what they want to accomplish.

1. **Discover intent.** Use the request and available context to identify
   the intended outcome, who it is for, and what success looks like. When
   that information is missing, ask one focused question about purpose or
   intended use before proposing features or an approach. Knowing the app
   genre does not tell you why your partner wants it. Gathering missing
   requirements does not ask them to authorize the task again.
2. **Write back your understanding.** Summarize the intended outcome,
   relevant constraints, and success criteria in a short note your partner
   can assess. Separate what they said from assumptions. Invite correction
   and incorporate their answer before treating this as the design brief.
3. **Carry intent into the design.** Preserve the agreed understanding in
   the selected path's design artifact: the written spec for architectural
   work, or the in-chat design/probe for bounded work and spikes. Check
   proposed features and technical choices against that understanding.

When the request already supplies the purpose and constraints, reflect
that understanding instead of asking the same questions again. Keep the
note concise; its accuracy and the opportunity to correct it matter.

<HARD-GATE>
Before taking any implementation action, including invoking an
implementation skill, writing product code, scaffolding, installing
product dependencies, or creating an external project, complete the
selected path's prerequisites:

- Spike: the human partner approves the question and probe.
- Bounded: the human partner approves the short in-chat design.
- Architectural: the human partner reviews and approves the written spec,
  then reviews the written implementation plan and selects its execution
  method. Conversational design approval only permits writing the spec;
  written-spec approval only permits invoking writing-plans.

A reply approves the stage actually presented. Approval of an idea or
feature scope does not approve artifacts that do not exist yet. Resume
at the earliest incomplete stage; do not turn one approval into permission
to skip the rest of the selected path. Read-only project exploration is
allowed while those prerequisites remain incomplete.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving the required design
before implementation. A bounded change may need only two sentences in
chat. A new todo-list project is architectural and requires the written
spec and planning handoffs. Scale the artifact to the selected path;
complete that path's reviews before implementation.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Follow the selected path: a bounded change gets a short chat design; an architectural change gets the written spec and planning handoffs. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

input.content:
# Design: how memories attach to trails (COR-2110)

Status: draft for review. Owner: evis. 2026-10-14.

## Problem

Memories (durable facts) are keyed by **branch name** at every layer:

- Local store: `facts/<slug>-<sha256(branch)[:4]>/facts.ndjson` (`internal/cli/facts.go`, `factsBranchRelDir`).
- Hosted head: `GET/POST /api/v1/repos/{repoID}/brain/facts?branch=<name>` — one CAS blob head per `(repo, branch name)` (`internal/factsync/httpserver.go`).
- Sync covers the current branch + default branch, on daemon tick, session-end hook, and `connect` (`internal/cli/watch.go`, `hook_cmd.go`). The plugin has **zero trail awareness**.

Branch names are ephemeral and the key breaks three ways:

1. **Rename.** Conductor auto-renames placeholder branches as a matter of routine. Local facts are stranded in the old directory; the hosted head is stranded under the old name; the new name starts empty. Memories "disappear".
2. **Delete after merge.** The hosted head survives, but nothing points to it; a trail-UI lookup by live branch returns an empty list (reported). Reviewer context is lost exactly when the trail becomes read-only history.
3. **Recycle.** A new branch reuses a deleted name: the first sync pulls the old trail's facts into the new local store and publishes new facts into the old head. Cross-contamination (reported from the branch auto-deletion/restoration work).

Two identities are already stable and should carry the design:

- **Fact identity**: content-derived (`sha256(normalized text + sorted paths)`), branch excluded (`factmerge/record.go`). Not the problem.
- **Trail identity**: stable ULID; trails record `branch` AND `original_branch`, so the platform already tracks a trail's branch rename, plus `base`, `merged_at`, status.

Recorded constraints (Brain recall, approved brainstore design):
- Memories must support every branch/trail and repo; statement-level attribution; per-repo, region-local storage.
- Preserve the existing Brain client and sync protocol until hosted memory works end to end.
- Conflict resolution belongs to a future async server pipeline; until then, keep-both.
- Entire is the source of truth; everything else is a pushed, idempotently-updated projection.

## Design principle

**The branch name is a mutable alias, never the durable key.** Durable attachment scopes are:

- **trail scope** — keyed by trail ULID, for feature-branch work;
- **repo-default scope** — one per repo, for the base branch, detached HEAD, and exploration; this backs the repo-level Memories page.

The client keeps publishing by `(repo, branch)` (wire protocol unchanged, per the locked decision). **Scope resolution is server-side**, where trails live.

## Server model (brainstore + entire-api)

### Alias resolution

New table `branch_alias (repo_id, branch_name, scope_id, generation, created_at, released_at)`. On publish or pull for branch B:

1. An **open** trail exists with `branch == B` → alias to that trail's scope.
2. B is the repo default branch (or the sync fell back to it: detached HEAD, no branch) → repo-default scope.
3. Otherwise → an anonymous branch scope `(B, generation)`; `generation` increments each time the name is re-bound after release, so a recycled name never touches a prior generation's head.

The alias table is a **pushed projection** of trail lifecycle events (created / branch-renamed / merged / closed) from entire-api — same pattern as entire-search, and consistent with "Entire is the source of truth". Brainstore never polls git.

### Lifecycle transitions

- **Trail created after facts already synced** (session-end fires before the first push creates the trail): the trail-created event **re-homes** the branch's anonymous scope into the trail scope via the shared `factmerge` merge — deterministic, idempotent, keep-both. This also covers "sync first, trail later" ordering generally; no client change needed.
- **Trail branch renamed**: event updates the alias row; the scope and its facts ride along. Nothing moves, nothing is lost.
- **Trail merged**: the trail scope is **frozen** — facts stay attached to the trail forever (the reviewer use-case: trail UI reads by trail ID, so a deleted branch can never empty the list). Active facts are **promoted** into the repo-default scope with `factmerge.Promote` keep-both semantics (conflicts accepted together; async resolution pipeline later, per the recorded decision). The alias row is released → the name is free; recycling it starts generation+1.
- **Trail closed without merge**: scope frozen, **no** promote, alias released.
- **Force-push**: scope key is the trail ULID, not a SHA — storage unaffected. Anchors referencing rewritten commits become unverifiable, which is already the local `verify` semantics.
- **Retraction after facts appeared on a trail**: unchanged — the head is authoritative for retirements and lifecycle moves one way (active → retired, never revival; `mergeHostedFactsIntoLocal`). The trail UI renders retracted facts as retracted (or hides them); the frozen post-merge scope still accepts status-only advances so a retraction recorded later propagates.
- **Same fact on multiple branches/trails**: expected; content ID makes it the same statement in each scope. Promote into repo-default dedupes by ID; UIs collapse by ID where both scopes are shown.

### Read model

- **Trail UI**: `memories for trail <ULID>` → the trail scope head (never keyed by branch). Statement-level attribution comes free: each record carries author (server-stamped) and provenance anchors (`SessionID`, `CheckpointID`), which the trail already knows how to link. A finer per-checkpoint grouping (join anchors → checkpoints → trail timeline) is a read-model refinement, not a storage change — defer.
- **Repo Memories page**: the repo-default scope head.
- Both stay behind the `trail-memories` flag until exposure flips.

## Local model (plugin)

Keep branch-name keying (local UX is branch-first: `--branch`, blind-spot notes, promote flow) and fix the two local failure modes with a small **lineage record** per branch directory — `lineage.json`: branch-creation commit (merge-base with default at first write), last-seen HEAD, hosted scope id once known (returned by the server on sync, additive response field).

- **Rename detection**: on sync/brief, current branch has no facts dir, but a dir's recorded lineage matches HEAD's history and its branch name no longer exists in git → one-time directory move. Facts follow the rename.
- **Recycle detection**: facts dir exists for the current branch, but its recorded creation commit is not an ancestor of HEAD (or its recorded scope id differs from what the server resolves) → archive the dir (facts preserved, not deleted) and start fresh.

ponytail: lineage detection is heuristic (ancestry checks, no reflog parsing); the upgrade path is the host CLI telling the plugin the trail id directly once a plugin↔host trail channel exists.

## Upload scope and triggers

- **What uploads**: unchanged — the branch's full active fact set (read-merge-CAS), `SanitizeForEgress` clears author; server stamps attribution. Facts need **no** trail and **no** feature branch to upload: main / detached HEAD / trail-less branches land in repo-default or an anonymous branch scope and still surface on the repo Memories page.
- **When** (today): daemon tick (current + default branch), session-end hook, connect.
- **Add**: a throttled async sync on **post-commit** (the host CLI already hooks commits for checkpoints), so facts distilled mid-session reach the trail while review is happening, not only at session end.
- **Staleness budget**: a trail page may lag local state by ≤ one daemon tick (minutes); a commit or session end tightens that to seconds. Server-side re-homing (trail events) removes the other staleness source — facts synced before the trail existed appear on the trail without any client action.

## Explicitly rejected

- **Client stamps trail IDs** (plugin asks host CLI which trail the branch belongs to): adds a plugin↔host dependency and still needs server-side re-homing for the "trail created after sync" ordering — so it buys nothing v1 needs. Revisit as the lineage-heuristic upgrade path.
- **SHA-keyed heads** (branch + HEAD commit): HEAD moves every commit; merge-base generations break on force-push. Trail ULID + generation covers the same cases without a moving key.
- **Deleting trail memories when the branch deletes**: the opposite of the reviewer use-case; merge freezes, never deletes.

## Implementation tickets (after design approval)

1. brainstore: scope + branch_alias model, generation semantics, migration of existing `(repo, branch)` heads to anonymous scopes.
2. entire-api → brainstore trail lifecycle events (created / renamed / merged / closed) + re-homing and promote-on-merge.
3. Trail UI + repo Memories read models by scope (behind `trail-memories`).
4. Plugin: lineage.json + rename/recycle detection; accept scope id in sync response (additive).
5. Plugin: post-commit throttled sync trigger.

## Open questions

1. **Promote-on-merge policy**: auto keep-both promote into repo-default (recommended; consistent with the recorded conflict decision and v1's cut of hosted review-queue endpoints) vs. holding merged-trail facts for review before they hit the repo page.
2. **Anonymous branch scopes on the repo page**: show trail-less branch facts on the repo Memories page, or only repo-default + merged-trail promotions? (Recommend: repo-default only in v1; anonymous scopes are reachable via `--branch` sync but not surfaced.)
3. Closed-without-merge trails: should their facts be promotable manually later?

## Problem

Branch names are ephemeral and the `(repo, branch name)` key breaks three ways:

1. **Rename** (Conductor does this routinely): local facts stranded in the old dir, hosted head stranded under the old name, new name starts empty.
2. **Delete after merge**: the hosted head survives but nothing points to it; the trail UI's branch lookup returns an empty list (reported).
3. **Recycle**: a new branch reusing a deleted name pulls the old trail's facts and publishes into the old head — cross-contamination (reported from branch auto-deletion/restoration work).

Recorded constraints (Brain recall, approved brainstore design): per-repo region-local storage; statement-level attribution; preserve the client sync protocol until hosted memory works e2e; conflicts are keep-both until the async resolution pipeline exists; Entire is the source of truth, everything else is a pushed idempotent projection.

## Principle

**The branch name is a mutable alias, never the durable key.** Durable scopes: **trail scope** (keyed by trail ULID) and **repo-default scope** (one per repo — base branch, detached HEAD, exploration; backs the repo Memories page). The client keeps publishing by `(repo, branch)` — wire protocol unchanged. **Scope resolution is server-side**, where trails live.

## Server model (brainstore + entire-api)

`branch_alias (repo_id, branch_name, scope_id, generation, created_at, released_at)`, maintained as a **pushed projection of trail lifecycle events** (created / branch-renamed / merged / closed) from entire-api — same pattern as entire-search. Resolution on publish/pull for branch B:

1. Open trail with `branch == B` → that trail's scope.
2. B is the default branch (or the sync fell back to it) → repo-default scope.
3. Otherwise → anonymous branch scope `(B, generation)`; generation increments on each re-bind after release, so a recycled name never touches a prior generation's head.

Lifecycle:

- **Trail created after facts already synced** (session-end fires before first push): the trail-created event **re-homes** the anonymous scope into the trail scope via the shared factmerge merge (deterministic, idempotent, keep-both). Covers "sync first, trail later" with no client change.
- **Trail branch renamed**: alias row updates; facts ride along.
- **Trail merged**: trail scope **frozen** — facts stay attached to the trail forever (reviewer use-case; the UI reads by trail ID, so a deleted branch can never empty the list). Active facts **promote** into repo-default with keep-both semantics. Alias released → name free; recycling starts generation+1.
- **Trail closed without merge**: frozen, no promote, alias released.
- **Force-push**: scope key is the trail ULID, not a SHA — storage unaffected; anchors on rewritten commits become unverifiable (existing `verify` semantics).
- **Retraction after appearing on a trail**: unchanged — head is authoritative for retirements, lifecycle moves one way; frozen scopes still accept status-only advances.
- **Same fact on multiple branches/trails**: expected; content ID dedupes at promote and collapses in UIs.

Read model: trail UI reads the trail scope head by ULID; repo Memories page reads repo-default. Statement-level attribution comes from server-stamped authors + provenance anchors already on every record. Both behind `trail-memories`.

## Local model (plugin)

Keep branch-name keying (local UX is branch-first) and add a per-branch-dir `lineage.json`: branch-creation commit (merge-base at first write), last-seen HEAD, hosted scope id once known (additive sync-response field). Rename detection: no facts dir for current branch + a dir whose lineage matches HEAD's history and whose branch no longer exists → one-time move. Recycle detection: dir exists but its creation commit is not an ancestor of HEAD (or scope id mismatch) → archive (never delete) and start fresh. Heuristic by design; upgrade path is the host CLI telling the plugin the trail id directly.

- What uploads: unchanged (full active set, read-merge-CAS, SanitizeForEgress). Facts need **no trail and no feature branch**: main / detached HEAD / trail-less branches land in repo-default or an anonymous scope.

## Rejected

- Client stamps trail IDs (plugin↔host dependency, and re-homing is needed anyway for ordering).
- SHA-keyed heads (HEAD moves every commit; merge-base generations break on force-push).
- Deleting trail memories when the branch deletes (opposite of the reviewer use-case; merge freezes, never deletes).

2. Repo Memories page: repo-default only in v1 (recommended), or also anonymous branch scopes?

Design update after review with Evis + reading the brainstore repo:

**Schema confirmation**: `branch` is in the primary key of every brainstore table (`brain_fact_heads (repo_id, branch)`, `brain_facts (repo_id, branch, fact_id)`, `brain_fact_events`), and `GET /memories` filters `WHERE repo_id = $1 AND branch = $2`. The scope model replaces `branch` with `scope_id` in these keys, with `branch_alias` resolving names; migration is small (single init migration, exposure off, existing heads become generation-0 anonymous scopes).

**Decisions**:
1. Promote-on-merge: auto keep-both promote into repo-default. ✅
2. Closed-without-merge trails: facts go away — never promoted, no manual promote path; readable only on the closed trail's historical page, GC-eligible later. ✅

**Still open**: whether the repo Memories page shows anonymous (trail-less, non-main) branch scopes, or repo-default only (recommended for v1).

content.text:
Decisions 1 and 3 are folded into the design (doc + ticket comment updated), and brainstore confirmed the diagnosis: `branch` is in the primary key of all four tables, and `/memories` filters `WHERE repo_id AND branch` — post-merge the rows still exist, but no caller holds a name that finds them. Migration is cheap since there's one init migration and exposure is off: existing heads become generation-0 anonymous scopes.

On **question 2**, here's what I meant. Some facts get synced from a branch that has **no trail and isn't main** — someone experimenting on a local branch they never push, or work that hasn't created a trail yet. Those facts land in an "anonymous branch scope" in brainstore (they have to land somewhere, since uploads can't wait for a trail to exist). The question is only about the **repo-level Memories page**: should it show those work-in-progress facts too, or just the repo-default scope (main-line facts plus everything promoted from merged trails)?

My recommendation: **repo-default only in v1.** Trail-less branch facts are unreviewed work-in-progress; they surface naturally once a trail is created (re-homing) or when the work merges (promotion), and they stay fully usable locally via `--branch` sync in the meantime. Showing them on the repo page would also mean the page accumulates noise from abandoned experiments.

If that works for you, the design is complete and I'll cut the five implementation tickets (brainstore scope/alias model + migration, trail lifecycle events + re-homing/promote, read models behind `trail-memories`, plugin lineage detection, post-commit sync trigger).

input.title: brainstore: re-key memories from branch name to scope_id + branch_alias table
input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design (see its comments for the full design).

Branch names are ephemeral (renamed, deleted on merge, recycled); today `branch` is in the primary key of every brainstore table. Replace it with a durable `scope_id`:

- Scope kinds: `trail` (trail ULID), `repo-default` (one per repo), `anon` (branch name + generation, for trail-less non-default branches).
- New `branch_alias (repo_id, branch_name, scope_id, generation, created_at, released_at)`; resolution on publish/pull: open trail with this branch → trail scope; default branch or fallback → repo-default; else anon scope. A re-bound name after release gets generation+1, so a recycled branch name never touches a prior generation's head.
- Re-key `brain_fact_heads`, `brain_facts`, `brain_fact_events` from `(repo_id, branch)` to `(repo_id, scope_id)`; keep branch as display metadata.
- Migration: existing `(repo_id, branch)` heads become generation-0 anon scopes (default branch → repo-default). Single init migration exists and exposure is off behind `trail-memories`, so this is cheap now.

Client wire protocol unchanged: the plugin keeps publishing by `(repo, branch)`; resolution is entirely server-side.

input.title: entire-api → brainstore: trail lifecycle events drive memory scope re-homing and promote-on-merge
input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design. Depends on the brainstore scope_id/branch_alias re-key.

Push trail lifecycle events (created / branch-renamed / merged / closed) from entire-api into brainstore as an idempotent projection (same pattern as entire-search):

- **created**: re-home the branch's anon scope into the trail scope via the shared factmerge merge (deterministic, keep-both). Covers facts synced before the trail existed — session-end sync often fires before the first push creates the trail.
- **branch-renamed**: update the alias row; facts ride along.
- **merged**: freeze the trail scope (facts stay attached to the trail permanently), auto keep-both promote active facts into repo-default (decided on COR-2110), release the alias.
- **closed without merge**: freeze, NO promote (decided: these facts never reach repo-default, no manual promote path; GC-eligible later), release the alias.

Frozen scopes still accept status-only advances so a retraction recorded locally after merge propagates (lifecycle stays one-way: active → retired).

input.title: Trail UI memories by trail ULID + repo Memories page on repo-default scope (behind trail-memories)
input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design. Depends on the brainstore scope model.

- Trail page memories tab queries by **trail ULID** (the trail scope), never by branch name — a deleted or renamed branch can no longer empty the list, and merged/closed trails keep their memories as a permanent record for reviewers.
- Repo-level Memories page reads the **repo-default scope only** (decided on COR-2110): main-line facts plus promotions from merged trails. Anonymous (trail-less branch) scopes are not surfaced.
- Statement-level attribution from server-stamped author handles + provenance anchors (session/checkpoint IDs) already on each record.
- Everything stays behind the `trail-memories` flag.

input.title: entire-brain plugin: branch lineage record — rename/recycle detection for the local fact store
input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design.

The local fact store is keyed by branch name (`facts/<slug>-<hash(branch)>/facts.ndjson`), so a rename strands facts and a recycled name resurfaces unrelated ones. Keep branch-first keying (local UX: `--branch`, blind-spot notes, promote flow) and add a per-branch-dir `lineage.json`: branch-creation commit (merge-base with default at first write), last-seen HEAD, hosted scope id once known (additive field on the sync response).

- **Rename**: current branch has no facts dir, but a dir's lineage matches HEAD's history and its branch no longer exists in git → one-time directory move.
- **Recycle**: dir exists but its creation commit is not an ancestor of HEAD (or scope id mismatches the server's resolution) → archive the dir (never delete) and start fresh.

Heuristic by design (ancestry checks, no reflog parsing); upgrade path is the host CLI handing the plugin the trail id directly.

input.title: entire-brain plugin: throttled post-commit hosted fact sync trigger
input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design.

Hosted fact sync currently runs on daemon tick, session-end hook, and connect — so facts distilled mid-session reach the trail only after the session ends or the next tick. Add a throttled, async sync on post-commit (the host CLI already hooks commits for checkpoint capture), covering current + default branch like the existing triggers.

Staleness budget after this: seconds after a commit or session end, ≤ one daemon tick otherwise. Must follow `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`'s never-fails discipline (soft-fail to stderr, never block the commit).

Done — repo-default-only is locked in, the design doc and ticket are updated, and implementation tickets **COR-2123 → COR-2127** are cut (brainstore re-key, trail events, read models/UI, plugin lineage, post-commit trigger). Here's the end-to-end workflow as designed:

## Life of a memory

**1. Birth.** A fact is either distilled from a session transcript or authored with `entire brain remember`. Its ID is `sha256(normalized text + sorted taxonomy paths)` — pure content. The same statement produces the same ID on any machine, any branch, any day; dedupe is a map lookup. The record also carries provenance anchors (session ID, checkpoint ID, transcript line) and a `branch` field, but neither is part of identity.

**2. Local storage.** The fact lands in `facts/<branch-slug>-<hash>/facts.ndjson` — keyed by branch *name*, because the local UX is branch-first (`--branch`, promote, blind-spot notes). New per COR-2126: each directory gets a `lineage.json` (branch-creation merge-base, last-seen HEAD, hosted scope id). If the branch gets renamed, the plugin notices the orphaned dir whose lineage matches HEAD and moves it; if the name was recycled, it notices the lineage *doesn't* match and archives the old dir instead of mixing.

**3. Upload.** Triggers: session-end hook, daemon tick, `connect`, and (new, COR-2127) a throttled post-commit hook — each syncs the current branch plus the default branch. The client publishes the branch's full active fact set via read-merge-CAS to `POST /repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance?branch=<name>`. **The client still speaks branch names and knows nothing about trails** — the wire protocol doesn't change. Author fields are stripped on egress; the server stamps attribution from the token.

**4. Server-side keying (the core change).** Brainstore stops storing by branch name. On every publish/pull it resolves the name through `branch_alias` into a durable **scope**, and the tables (`brain_fact_heads`, `brain_facts`, `brain_fact_events`) key on `(repo_id, scope_id)`:
- open trail exists for this branch → **trail scope** (keyed by the trail's ULID)
- default branch, or the detached-HEAD fallback → **repo-default scope** (one per repo)
- anything else → **anonymous scope** `(branch name, generation)`

So facts never need a trail or even a feature branch to upload — exploration on main goes straight to repo-default.

**5. Trails drive the lifecycle** via events pushed from entire-api (idempotent projection, like entire-search):
- **Trail created** — often *after* facts already synced, since session-end fires before the first push — the branch's anonymous scope is merged (keep-both, deterministic) into the trail scope. This re-homing is why the client never needs to learn trail IDs.
- **Branch renamed** — the alias row updates; the scope and its facts don't move.
- **Merged** — the trail scope **freezes** (memories stay on the trail forever, for reviewers), active facts auto-promote keep-both into repo-default, and the alias is released. A recycled name binds to generation+1: a fresh scope, zero contamination.
- **Closed without merge** — freeze, no promote ever, GC-eligible later.

**6. Reads.** The trail page queries by trail ULID — a deleted branch can never empty it again. The repo Memories page reads repo-default only. Teammates' plugins pull their current branch's resolved scope and merge it into their local store (retirements propagate one-way; a locally retracted fact never revives).

One sentence version: **fact identity is content, fact attachment is a server-resolved scope, and the branch name is just the address the client happens to write on the envelope.**

input.description:
Part of the COR-2110 design.

Hosted fact sync currently runs on daemon tick, session-end hook, and connect — so facts distilled mid-session reach the trail only after the session ends or the next tick. Give the plugin a per-commit signal.

**Finding (2026-10-14): both halves of the plumbing already exist, but the host half never merged.**

- Plugin side (on entire-brain main): `entire brain memory notify --event {session_start|checkpoint|session_end}` (`internal/cli/memory_cmd.go`) — content-free lifecycle hints that nudge the memory worker.
- Host side: `brainnotify` package (`entireio/cli` commit 73a92e8da, branch `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints`, **not merged to main** as of 2026-10-14) — detached best-effort `entire brain memory notify` calls, including `EventCheckpoint` fired at checkpoint creation (= every commit; the host already runs a post-commit git hook for checkpoint capture).

Scope of this ticket therefore:
1. Land (or re-cut) the host-side `brainnotify` lifecycle hints so the plugin receives a checkpoint hint per commit.
2. In the plugin, make the `checkpoint` hint also trigger a throttled `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` (today the notify path only nudges the conversation-projection worker; hosted sync is wired to watch tick + session-end only).

Must follow `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`'s never-fails discipline (detached, soft-fail to stderr, never block the commit or the host hook).

Staleness budget after this: seconds after a commit or session end, ≤ one daemon tick otherwise.

content.text:
## 1. Post-commit events from the CLI to the plugin — designed, half-shipped

Both halves of the plumbing exist, but **the host half never merged**:

- **Plugin side (on main today):** `entire brain memory notify --event {session_start | checkpoint | session_end}` (`internal/cli/memory_cmd.go`) — a content-free lifecycle hint endpoint, explicitly described as "the endpoint host adapters call across the external Entire CLI boundary". Right now it only nudges the conversation-projection memory worker, not hosted fact sync.
- **Host side (NOT on main):** the `entireio/cli` branch `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints` (commit `73a92e8da`) adds a `brainnotify` package that fires detached, best-effort `entire brain memory notify` calls — including an **`EventCheckpoint`** at checkpoint creation, which is per-commit, since the host already installs a `post-commit` git hook for checkpoint capture. I verified against today's checkout (`83e283f17`, 2026-10-14): nothing on cli main invokes the plugin on commit or session end.

So the answer is: the *moment* exists (host post-commit hook), the *channel* exists (memory notify), but the wire between them is sitting on an unmerged branch. I updated COR-2127 accordingly: land/re-cut `brainnotify` host-side, then make the `checkpoint` hint also trigger a throttled `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`. Worth checking why `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints` stalled before building on it.

## 2. What a trail scope is, and how memories attach

A **trail scope** is just a bucket in brainstore whose `scope_id` is the trail's ULID — the fact head and `brain_facts` rows re-keyed under the trail instead of under a branch name. Nothing fancier.

How a memory ends up in it — and yes, **the branch name is the join, but only as a momentary lookup, never as the stored key**:

- The client syncs "here are the facts for branch B" (it stays trail-unaware). Brainstore resolves B through `branch_alias` *at that instant*: is there an **open** trail in this repo whose current branch is B? If yes, the facts land in that trail's scope. If B is the default branch, repo-default. Otherwise an anonymous `(B, generation)` bucket.
- If facts synced *before* the trail existed (session-end usually fires before the first push creates the trail), the trail-created event re-homes the anonymous bucket into the trail scope.

The difference from today: currently the branch name **is the storage key**, so it has to stay correct forever — and it doesn't. In the design it's only consulted at write time against live trail state, then the durable key is the ULID. Once attached, rename/delete/recycle can't touch anything: reads go by trail ULID, a renamed trail branch just updates the alias row, and a recycled name only ever matches a *newly opened* trail or a fresh generation — never a frozen old scope.

The branch-name join is sound at that instant because an open trail ↔ branch binding is one-to-one in the platform. The finer alternative — joining each fact's provenance anchors (session/checkpoint IDs) to the trail's checkpoint membership — is noted in the design as a read-model refinement for per-checkpoint attribution, but it isn't needed for attachment.
can we diagram this?

Yes — here it is in three views: the write path, the trail lifecycle, and the read path. (ASCII so it renders in the terminal, Linear, and the doc; added to both.)

**1. Write path — where a fact lands**

```
DEVELOPER MACHINE                              SERVER (region-local)
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ agent session               │
│   distill / `remember`      │
│          │                  │
│          ▼                  │
│ local fact store            │
│  facts/<branch>-<hash>/     │
│    facts.ndjson             │
│    lineage.json ◄─ rename / │
│                    recycle  │
│                    detection│
└──────────┬──────────────────┘
           │ triggers: session-end hook · daemon tick
           │           · connect · post-commit (new)
           ▼
  POST /repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance?branch=B
           │   client knows only (repo, branch) — no trail awareness
           ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ brainstore                                      │
│                                                 │
│  branch_alias: (repo,"B") ──► scope_id          │
│   resolved at write time:                       │
│     open trail with branch B ──► TRAIL scope    │
│     B == default / fallback  ──► REPO-DEFAULT   │
│     else                     ──► ANON (B, genN) │
│                                                 │
│  heads / facts / events keyed (repo, scope_id)  │
└───────────────────────▲─────────────────────────┘
                        │ trail lifecycle events
                        │ (pushed projection)
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              │ entire-api trails │
              └───────────────────┘
```

**2. Trail lifecycle — how scopes move**

```
 ANON scope (B, gen0)        TRAIL scope (ULID)         REPO-DEFAULT scope
        │                           │                           │
        │  trail created for B      │                           │
        ├—— re-home (keep-both) ——►│                           │
        │                           │                           │
        │                           │ branch renamed:           │
        │                           │   alias row updates,      │
        │                           │   facts don't move        │
        │                           │                           │
        │                           │ MERGED:                   │
        │                           │   freeze scope ─ memories │
        │                           │   stay on trail forever   │
        │                           ├—— promote actives ———————►│
        │                           │   (keep-both, auto)       │
        │                           │   alias released          │
        │                           │                           │
 branch "B" recycled                │ CLOSED w/o merge:         │
  → gen1, fresh empty scope         │   freeze, NO promote,     │
        │                           │   GC-eligible             │
```

**3. Read path**

```
trail page     ──── by trail ULID ─────► TRAIL scope      (immune to branch
                                                           rename/delete)
repo Memories  ──── repo-default only ─► REPO-DEFAULT     (main-line facts +
                                                           merged-trail promotions)
teammate sync  ──── GET ?branch=B ─────► resolved scope ─► merged into their
                                                           local branch store
```

The thing to hold onto across all three: the branch name appears only on the arrows (a momentary lookup against live trail state), never inside a box — every box is keyed by content hash (facts), trail ULID, or repo.

content.text:
Anchors already cross the wire — `SanitizeForEgress` strips only local file coordinates (transcript path/line) and keeps `SessionID`, `Commit`, `CheckpointID`, `TurnID`. Brainstore just doesn't project them into the `brain_facts` table. That matters a lot for what follows.

## First principles

Start with what a memory *is*: a durable statement produced by **work**. The work has a natural identity chain that Entire already models end to end:

```
fact ──anchors──► session ──► checkpoint ──► commit ──► trail / main history
```

A fact is born knowing its session and checkpoint (distill stamps them today). Checkpoints bind to commits. Trails are *defined* as a set of checkpoints/commits. So the deterministic, easy-to-look-up key you're asking for already exists: **the provenance anchor**. The branch never appears in this chain — it's a mutable *label* on the workspace where the chain happened. The reason branch feels wrong to you is that it is: we've been using the label as the key.

The second realization: the branch currently does **two unrelated jobs**, and they deserve different answers:

1. **Transport** — "which working set do I merge into when I sync?" (the CAS head)
2. **Attachment** — "which trail/page shows this memory?"

The scope/alias design fixed both with one mechanism. First principles says split them.

### Attachment: a join, not a mapping

A memory belongs to trail T iff **any of its anchors reference a session/checkpoint/commit that belongs to T**. That's it. No alias table, no generations, no re-homing, no promote events — because:

- **Rename / delete / recycle become non-events.** Anchors are immutable history; nothing can strand or contaminate them.
- **"Memories show up with commits" falls out for free.** A fact anchored to checkpoint X renders next to that commit in the trail timeline — that's the per-commit display you want, not just a flat trail-level list.
- **"On main" is derived, not evented.** A fact appears on the repo Memories page when its anchoring commits are reachable from the default branch. Merge a trail → its commits become ancestors of main → its facts are repo-visible. No promote step; the predicate just becomes true. Deterministic and self-healing (a lost event can't desync it).

### The no-branch / no-commit ladder

Each rung has a natural answer because attachment keys on work, not workspace:

| Situation | Anchor available | Where it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Normal trail work | session + checkpoint + commit | trail, next to its commit |
| Fact distilled at session end, after last commit | session (+ last checkpoint) | trail, via session membership |
| Detached HEAD | session + checkpoint | wherever those commits land |
| Exploration on main | session + checkpoint on main | repo page directly |
| Authored mid-session, no commit yet | session | attaches when the session's commits/trail appear; until then "recent/unattached" repo pool |
| `remember` outside any session, no commit | author + time only | repo pool |

The ladder degrades gracefully: the less history context a fact has, the more repo-global it is. That's the *correct* semantic, not a fallback hack.

### Transport, separately

If attachment no longer reads branch keys, the sync head's key only needs to be *hygienic*, not *meaningful*. Two options: keep branch-named heads and fix recycling (generation marker — small), or go further and drop set-heads for **per-fact idempotent upsert** (fact ID is content-derived; status lifecycle is one-way; anchors union). Per-fact upsert makes sync naturally idempotent and kills the set-CAS machinery, but it rewrites the wire protocol and local merge path — the single biggest cost on the table. Notably, per-branch *truth* also dissolves: a fact's status (active/retracted) is arguably a repo-level property; branch isolation locally is really about keeping *unreviewed* facts out of main's brief, which the "reachable from main" predicate expresses better than per-branch copies.

### Events

The checkpoint event is both the **trigger** and the **join key** — commit → checkpoint captured → notify plugin → sync facts with anchors → trail page shows them beside that commit. One concept doing both jobs is usually the sign the model is right.

## Diff against the approved scope/alias design

| | Scope/alias (approved) | Anchor-based (first principles) |
|---|---|---|
| Memory→trail key | branch name at write time, made durable as trail ULID | anchors joined to trail membership at read time |
| Machinery | alias table, generations, re-home, promote, release — ~5 lifecycle events | one join + one reachability predicate; trail events unneeded |
| Rename/recycle/delete | handled by enumerated machinery | non-events by construction |
| Promote on merge | event copies facts into repo-default | derived: anchor commits reachable from main |
| Per-commit display | deferred refinement | native |
| Wire protocol | unchanged | unchanged **if** we keep heads as dumb transport; rewritten if we go per-fact |
| Brainstore change | new keying + alias | project anchors into `brain_facts` + join against core's checkpoint→trail data |
| New dependency | trail lifecycle events from entire-api | checkpoint/session→trail resolution from core (query or projection) |
| Weakness | branch is still the join at one instant; machinery can desync from events | anchor quality: distill anchors a whole session to its *latest* checkpoint today, so per-commit precision needs the turn→checkpoint mapping (schema has `TurnID` for this, Phase B); session-only facts attach late |

**My honest take:** the anchor model is the better foundation — it's the only one where your three requirements (deterministic key, memories-beside-commits, works with no branch/no commit) are properties of the model rather than features bolted on. The scope/alias design is a pragmatic approximation that mostly re-derives, via events, information the anchors already carry. The hybrid I'd actually build: **keep the existing set-head transport (branch-named heads demoted to dumb buckets, with the small recycle fix), project anchors into the read model, and compute all attachment — trail and repo page — by anchor join.** That drops most of COR-2123/2124's machinery, keeps the shipped protocol, and leaves per-fact transport as a later simplification if the heads ever hurt.

The two things to pressure-test before committing: how good distilled anchor precision actually is in prod data (session-end distill → everything anchored to the last checkpoint — fine for trail attachment, coarse for per-commit placement), and where the checkpoint→trail join runs (brainstore querying core vs. core pushing a projection vs. the BFF joining at read time — the BFF already has trail data, which might make brainstore's job purely "store facts with anchors").

Want me to rework the design doc and tickets around the anchor model, or dig into those two pressure-test questions first?

input.content:
# Design: how memories attach to trails (COR-2110) — anchor model

Status: v2, approved direction 2026-10-14 (supersedes the scope/alias v1 below in Appendix). Owner: evis. Tickets: COR-2123..2127 (updated to match).

## Two-sentence summary

A memory is keyed by the work that produced it — its provenance anchors (session + checkpoint + commit), stamped at creation and immutable — and every surface is a query over them: a trail shows facts anchored to its checkpoints/sessions beside the commit they came from, the repo page shows facts whose commits merged to main, and facts with less history degrade toward the repo pool. We push on the checkpoint event (same beat as the commit, so the memory appears next to it), with session-end and daemon tick covering the rungs that have no commit.

## Problem (unchanged from v1)

Memories are branch-name-keyed at every layer:

- Local store: `facts/<slug>-<sha256(branch)[:4]>/facts.ndjson` (`internal/cli/facts.go`).
- Hosted head: `GET/POST /api/v1/repos/{repoID}/brain/facts?branch=<name>` (`internal/factsync/httpserver.go`).
- Brainstore: `branch` is in the PK of `brain_fact_heads`, `brain_facts`, `brain_fact_events`; `/memories` filters `WHERE repo_id AND branch`.

Branch names are ephemeral: rename strands facts, post-merge delete empties the trail lookup, recycle cross-contaminates. The plugin has zero trail awareness.

## Principle

The branch does two unrelated jobs today. Split them:

1. **Transport** — which working set a sync merges into. Branch stays here, demoted to a dumb bucket label (with a small recycle-hygiene fix). Wire protocol unchanged.
2. **Attachment** — which trail/page shows a memory. Branch is removed entirely; attachment keys on the **provenance anchor chain**, which Entire already models end to end:

```
fact ──anchors──► session ──► checkpoint ──► commit ──► trail / main history
```

Anchors already cross the wire: `SanitizeForEgress` strips only local transcript path/line and keeps SessionID, Commit, CheckpointID, TurnID. Brainstore currently drops them from the read model — that projection is the main storage change.

## Attachment: a join, not a mapping

- A memory belongs to **trail T** iff any anchor references a session/checkpoint/commit in T's membership. Rendered beside the anchoring commit in the trail timeline.
- A memory is on the **repo Memories page** iff its anchoring commits are reachable from the default branch (merge makes this true automatically — no promote event), or it lives in the repo pool (bottom ladder rungs).
- Rename / delete / recycle of branches are **non-events**: anchors are immutable history.
- Trail merged: its commits become main-ancestors → facts become repo-visible, and stay on the trail (membership never changes). Trail closed without merge: its commits never reach main → facts stay only on the closed trail. Both v1 decisions (auto-promote; closed-trails-go-away) are now *derived*, not evented.
- Retraction: fact status is repo-global, one-way (active → retired), propagated by fact ID. A retracted fact renders as retracted everywhere its anchors place it.

## The no-branch / no-commit ladder

| Situation | Anchor available | Where it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Normal trail work | session + checkpoint + commit | trail, next to its commit |
| Fact distilled at session end, after last commit | session (+ last checkpoint) | trail, via session membership |
| Detached HEAD | session + checkpoint | wherever those commits land |
| Exploration on main | session + checkpoint on main | repo page directly |
| Authored mid-session, no commit yet | session | attaches when the session's commits/trail appear; until then "recent/unattached" repo pool |
| `remember` outside any session, no commit | author + time only | repo pool |

The ladder degrades gracefully: the less history context a fact has, the more repo-global it is.

## Upload scope and triggers

- What uploads: unchanged — the branch bucket's full active set, read-merge-CAS, SanitizeForEgress. Facts need no trail, no branch, no commit to upload.
- Triggers: **checkpoint event** (host `brainnotify` → `entire brain memory notify --event checkpoint`; host half on unmerged `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints`, see COR-2127) is the primary beat — the same event that creates the commit the memory will sit beside. Session-end hook, daemon tick, and connect remain for the no-commit rungs and as reconciliation.
- Staleness: seconds after a commit/session end; ≤ one tick otherwise. No event machinery can desync attachment — a lost event only delays upload, never misplaces a fact.

## Transport hygiene (small, replaces v1's scope re-key)

Heads stay keyed by `(repo, branch)` as dumb buckets, but a recycled branch name must not merge into a dead line's head: add a generation/lineage marker (e.g. branch-creation commit recorded with the head; mismatch → new head generation). Local store mirrors this with `lineage.json` rename/recycle detection (COR-2126). Contamination becomes a transport-hygiene issue only — reads never key on branch.

## Open questions (pressure-tests before implementation)

1. **Anchor precision**: distill anchors a whole session to its *latest* checkpoint (`distill_cmd.go` stamps `session.LatestCheckpoint`). Fine for trail attachment; coarse for per-commit placement. Per-commit precision needs the turn→checkpoint mapping (Anchor.TurnID exists, Phase B). Measure prod anchor quality first.
2. **Join location**: who resolves checkpoint/session→trail — the BFF at read time (it already has trail data; brainstore stays "facts with anchors"), core pushing a membership projection into brainstore, or brainstore querying core? Leaning BFF-first (zero new projections), revisit if query cost bites.
3. Repo-pool UX: how "recent/unattached" facts surface on the repo page (v1 can hide them).

## What this drops from v1

- `branch_alias` table, generations-as-attachment, re-homing, promote-on-merge event, alias release — all dissolved into the join + reachability predicate.
- Trail lifecycle event consumption in brainstore (COR-2124 repurposed to the attachment join).

## Appendix: v1 scope/alias design (superseded)

v1 modeled attachment as a server-side `branch→scope` alias (trail ULID / repo-default / anon+generation) maintained by trail lifecycle events, with freeze + auto keep-both promote on merge. Kept for reference in the COR-2110 comment history (2026-10-14). Decisions made under v1 that carry over with new mechanics: auto repo visibility on merge (now derived via reachability), closed-unmerged trails' facts never reach the repo page (derived), repo page shows no WIP branch facts (derived).

# Design: how memories attach to trails (COR-2110)

Version 2, approved 2026-10-14. Owner: evis. Implementation tickets: COR-2123 to COR-2127. Version 1 (scope/alias) is summarized at the end; v2 replaces it.

## Summary

A fact records which session, checkpoint, and commit produced it. These provenance anchors are written at creation and never change. Trail and repo pages find facts by querying these anchors. The branch name is no longer used to attach a fact to anything; it remains only as the sync bucket name and the local store key. Upload runs on the checkpoint event (per commit), on session end, and on the daemon tick.

## Problem

Memories are keyed by branch name at every layer:

- Local store: `facts/<slug>-<sha256(branch)[:4]>/facts.ndjson` (`internal/cli/facts.go`).
- Sync protocol: `GET/POST /api/v1/repos/{repoID}/brain/facts?branch=<name>` (`internal/factsync/httpserver.go`).
- Brainstore: `branch` is in the primary key of `brain_fact_heads`, `brain_facts`, and `brain_fact_events`. `/memories` filters `WHERE repo_id = $1 AND branch = $2`.

Branch names change. Three failure modes, all reported:

1. Rename (Conductor renames placeholder branches automatically): local facts stay in the old directory; the hosted head stays under the old name; the new name starts empty.
2. Delete after merge: the rows still exist under the old name, but no caller holds that name, so the trail UI gets an empty list.
3. Recycle: a new branch that reuses a deleted name syncs against the old head. The first sync pulls the old facts into the new local store and publishes new facts into the old head.

## Facts about the current system that the design uses

- Fact identity is `sha256(normalized text + sorted paths)`. Branch is not part of the identity (`factmerge/record.go`).
- Distill stamps each fact with provenance anchors: SessionID, CheckpointID, transcript position (`internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:1133`).
- Anchors cross the wire. `SanitizeForEgress` removes only the local transcript path and line; SessionID, Commit, CheckpointID, and TurnID stay in the synced blob (`internal/factsync/egress.go`).
- Brainstore currently drops anchors when it projects the blob into `brain_facts` rows. The migration has no anchor columns.
- The platform already maps checkpoints and sessions to trails. Trails have stable ULIDs.

## Design

The branch currently does two jobs. Separate them.

### Job 1: transport (which bucket a sync merges into)

Unchanged, with one fix. The client keeps publishing the full active fact set per `(repo, branch)` with read-merge-CAS. The fix: a recycled branch name must not merge into the previous branch's head. Store a lineage marker with each head (for example the branch-creation commit). If the marker does not match, start a new head instead of merging. The local store gets the same fix via a `lineage.json` file per branch directory (COR-2126): detect rename (move the directory) and recycle (archive the directory, start fresh).

The wire protocol does not change.

### Job 2: attachment (which trail or page shows a fact)

Drop the branch. Attach by anchors:

- A fact belongs to trail T if any of its anchors reference a session, checkpoint, or commit in T. The UI renders the fact next to the commit its anchor points to.
- A fact appears on the repo Memories page if its anchoring commits are reachable from the default branch, or if it has no session/commit anchors at all (the repo pool).

Consequences, each following directly from the fact that anchors are immutable:

- Branch rename, delete, and recycle have no effect on attachment. There is nothing to migrate or re-home.
- Trail merge needs no promote step. After the merge, the trail's commits are ancestors of main, so its facts satisfy the repo-page predicate. The facts also stay visible on the trail, because trail membership never changes.
- A trail closed without merging needs no cleanup step. Its commits never reach main, so its facts never appear on the repo page. They remain visible on the closed trail.
- A lost or delayed event can delay an upload. It cannot attach a fact to the wrong place, because attachment is computed from stored data at read time.

Fact status (active / superseded / retracted) is global per repo and moves one way (active → retired). A retracted fact renders as retracted on every surface its anchors place it.

### Attachment per situation

| Situation | Anchors present | Where the fact shows |
|---|---|---|
| Work on a trail branch | session + checkpoint + commit | on the trail, next to its commit |
| Distilled at session end, after the last commit | session + last checkpoint | on the trail, via session membership |
| Detached HEAD | session + checkpoint | wherever those commits end up |
| Work directly on main | session + checkpoint on main | repo page |
| Authored mid-session, before any commit | session | attaches when the session's commits/trail exist; until then, repo pool |
| `remember` outside any session | author + timestamp only | repo pool |

### Upload triggers

- Checkpoint event (per commit). This is the main trigger and the reason facts appear on the trail during review rather than after it. The plugin endpoint `entire brain memory notify --event checkpoint` exists on main (`internal/cli/memory_cmd.go`). The host-side caller (`brainnotify`, entireio/cli commit 73a92e8da) is on the unmerged branch `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints`. COR-2127 lands the host side and wires the checkpoint event to a throttled `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`.
- Session-end hook, daemon tick, and connect stay as they are. They cover facts with no commit and act as reconciliation if an event is missed.
- Expected staleness: seconds after a commit or session end; at most one daemon tick otherwise.

## Implementation tickets

1. COR-2123 — brainstore: add anchor columns (SessionID, CheckpointID, Commit, TurnID) to the `brain_facts` projection; add the head lineage marker for recycled branch names.
2. COR-2124 — the attachment join: fact anchors → trail membership, and the main-reachability predicate for the repo page. Includes deciding where the join runs (see open questions).
3. COR-2125 — trail UI (facts next to commits) and repo Memories page, behind the `trail-memories` flag.
4. COR-2126 — plugin: `lineage.json` rename/recycle detection for the local store.
5. COR-2127 — host `brainnotify` + plugin checkpoint-event sync trigger.

## Open questions

1. Anchor precision. Distill stamps every fact of a session with the session's latest checkpoint. That is enough to attach a fact to the right trail, but not always to the right commit within the trail. `Anchor.TurnID` plus the turn→checkpoint mapping gives per-commit precision later. Measure anchor quality on prod data before building per-commit rendering.
2. Where the join runs. Options: the BFF joins at read time (it already holds trail membership; brainstore stores facts with anchors and nothing else), core pushes a checkpoint→trail membership projection into brainstore, or brainstore queries core. Current lean: BFF at read time. Revisit if query cost is a problem.
3. Repo pool UX. How authored facts with no anchors appear on the repo page. V1 of the page can hide them.

## Superseded: version 1 (scope/alias)

V1 kept set-level attachment and moved the storage key from branch name to a server-resolved scope: trail ULID, repo-default, or anonymous (branch, generation). A `branch_alias` table, maintained from trail lifecycle events (created / renamed / merged / closed), mapped branch names to scopes; trail creation re-homed an anonymous scope into the trail scope, and trail merge froze the trail scope and copied active facts into repo-default.

V2 replaces this because the anchors already carry the attachment information: the alias table, generations for attachment, re-homing, and the promote event all reconstruct — through events that can be lost or arrive out of order — what the anchors state directly. The only part of v1 that survives is the recycle fix on transport heads, which is a storage-hygiene issue independent of attachment.

Decisions made under v1 that still hold, now derived instead of evented: merged trails' facts become repo-visible automatically; closed-unmerged trails' facts never become repo-visible; the repo page does not show work-in-progress branch facts.

Yes, we can get rid of it — and trying to answer your question exposed a real hole in v2 that makes removal the better option. Let me walk through it.

**What the fix protects.** Attachment no longer reads branch names, so recycle contamination cannot misplace anything in the UI. The remaining damage is local: when a new branch reuses a deleted name, the first pull downloads the old head and merges unrelated facts into the new branch's local store, where brief/recall serve them as context. That is the exact bug reported from the Conductor branch auto-delete work. The local `lineage.json` fix alone cannot stop it, because the next pull from the stale hosted head re-imports the old facts. So as long as pulls are served from branch-named heads, the server needs the marker.

**The branch-named head is the last remnant of the old model.** We removed the branch from attachment by replacing a stored mapping with a computed predicate. The same move works for transport:

- **Push:** per-fact idempotent upsert keyed `(repo, fact_id)` — union anchors, one-way status. No set head, no CAS, no merge, no marker.
- **Pull:** the client fetches the repo's fact delta (cursor by `updated_at`) and filters locally: keep facts whose anchor commits are reachable from my HEAD, plus facts from my own sessions. Reachability is a local `git merge-base --is-ancestor` check — the client has the commit graph, the server never needs it.

A recycled branch then pulls nothing stale by construction: the new branch's history does not contain the old trail's commits, so the old facts fail the filter. If the old trail *merged*, its commits are in the new branch's history — and then its facts are legitimately relevant, which is the correct behavior, not contamination.

**The hole this fixes.** V2 as written broke teammate distribution of merged facts, and I missed it. V1 moved merged facts into the repo-default head, which teammates pull on main. V2 dropped promote, but kept per-branch heads — so facts synced under `foo` never enter the `main` head, and a teammate on main never receives them locally. The repo *page* shows them (read-time predicate), but brief/recall on a teammate's machine never will. With heads, we'd have to reintroduce a promote event to fix this. With reachability-filtered pull, it's automatic: once the trail merges, its anchor commits are in every teammate's main history, so their next pull takes the facts.

**Costs.**
- Replaces the shipped sync protocol (`facts?branch=` / `facts/advance`). The "preserve the protocol until hosted memory works end to end" decision has been satisfied — e2e validated 2026-10-08 — and exposure is still off behind `trail-memories`, so this is the cheapest moment it will ever be.
- The set-level merge machinery (CAS, keep-both proposals at head level) goes away. Conflicts become "two active facts that disagree," which was already deferred to the async resolution pipeline.
- Local store: branch directories survive as a cache of the filtered view, and `lineage.json` (COR-2126) likely becomes unnecessary too — rename and recycle stop mattering locally for the same reason, since the view rebuilds from HEAD. That's a staged local refactor, not a blocker.

**Recommendation:** drop the branch heads. Transport becomes per-fact upsert up, reachability-filtered delta down — the same predicate everywhere. The lineage marker, the local rename/recycle detection, and the promote problem all disappear instead of being patched.

If you agree, I'll update the doc and rework the tickets (COR-2123 becomes the per-fact store + delta endpoint, COR-2126 likely folds away). Or if you want to keep the shipped protocol untouched for launch, the marker stays as the v2 stopgap — but then we must also add promote back for teammate distribution, which is the strongest argument against stopping halfway.
